Ashes are superior to wet bathing; in wet [bathing], the destruction of living beings is certain.
One should know wetness as Prakṛti, and Prakṛti as bondage.
For the abandoning of Prakṛti, bathing with ashes is prescribed,
as well as being sky-clad and pure, so that one may never be reborn.
Among yantras, it is the supreme yantra, other than which none exists;
six-limbed, granting all desires, revered by all the worlds,
pure, all-purifying, removing all sins, auspicious,
and increasing austerity—let them practice it with focused minds.
The yantra should be understood as sinless, and that is considered Prakṛti.
Bondage is declared to be threefold, and renunciation itself has its fruit;
therefore, for the abandoning of everything, one should practice this yantra,

And whoever, observing restraints here, bathes in ashes with vows subdued,
should stay even for a single muhūrta, shall go to the midst of the gaṇas.
Imperishable, immortal, freed from old age and disease,
he becomes a leader of Rudra's gaṇas and attains the sovereign power of yoga.
Even a person of willful conduct, exceedingly wicked in soul, who dwells here for a single day,
attains the fruit of an horse sacrifice and is freed from all sins.
Even a person of evil conduct, full of desire, who abandons his life-breaths here,
reaches the assembly of the gods and shall move among the gods.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then all those deities, having attained that supreme austerity,
performed the sacrificial ablution to Īśa, the Supreme Self.
Then, having accomplished their purpose, endowed with the power of great yoga,
all those celestials set their minds on going to Hari.
Approaching him who was blazing like the sun, O Vyāsa,
those mighty ones saw the imperishable Hari on Mount Hariścandra.

Rising up with speed towards them, O best of seers,
he swiftly descended from the peak and stood among them.
Then, delighted, meeting together fully with Hari,
they endowed that peak of the mountain with a reward:
‘Because Hari shone here as stainless as the moon
by means of great austerity, therefore this Lord of Mountains
shall be known as Hariścandra; of this there is no doubt.
And because a descent was made here by one who is not ordinary,
therefore let this precipice become holy in the world in every way.’
O lords of gods, whichever man, coming here, casts himself from this cliff,
shall go to Hari's exceedingly radiant world.
A person afflicted with disease, [even if] tainted by the great sins,
who gives up his life-breaths here, is also freed from great terror.
Whatever a man continually prays for here at the precipice,
all that he swiftly obtains—so it is declared.
Sanatkumāra said:
The knower of dharma who reads or listens to this [account of] Hariścandra and Puriścandra
destroys all his sin.
And whatever man, pure and free from malice, always reads this in an assembly of twice-born and gods,
he, stainless, blazing with brilliance like the sun, dwells in heaven like an immortal, foremost among them.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled ‘Description of Mount Hariścandra’, in the Skandapurāṇa.

Having reached that Puriścandra, Rāma, son of Śakti,

7.13.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the high-minded Lord, pleased, the source of words,
spoke these deep-toned words to the son of Jamadagni,
who was covered as if by kiṃśuka flowers, sprinkled as if with red sandalwood,
thus covered completely with blood,
flowing with red chalk like another king of mountains.
The god of gods said:
O son of Jamadagni, a great deed has been done by you today in battle,
wishing for the benefit of the gods, striking down the sons of Siṃhikā.
Pleased with this deed of yours, O mighty-armed one,
I grant seven boons; name them as you desire.
Rāma said:
O Lord, if you are pleased, grant me yourself, O Master,
the arising of all knowledge as set forth by all the Vedas.
May I be unslayable in battle; grant me the science of archery,
an axe that slays all, an unimpeded chariot,
a vast array of weapons, and imperishable immortality.
Grant these boons to me, O God; homage to you!

Sanatkumāra said:
As he was speaking thus, O Vyāsa, the blessed Hara smiled and said:
“All this will belong to you by my command. / 8.123.10
You shall observe the vow of the archery treatise for one year.

Then, having made the earth devoid of kṣatriyas, the best of the Bhṛgus,
by the grace of Mahādeva, shone like the lord of the three worlds. / 22
To him Śrī, Tuṣṭi, Dhṛti, Siddhi, Kīrti, and Yaśas,
Śraddhā, Medhā, Kṣānti, Anasūyā, and Prasaṃyama, / 23
Ūhā, Apohā, Tarka, Dama, and Śama—
all personified mothers approached the descendant of Bhṛgu. / 24
He then said to them all, “Enter into me without hesitation;
but let this ill-behaved Śrī remain far away!” / 25
Sanatkumāra said:
To him speaking thus, the virtuous Śrī said to the very powerful one:
“For what reason, O mighty-armed one, do you not welcome me who am difficult to attain?” / 26
Rāma said:
“You are fickle, intoxicating, and impermanent, O fair one.
Therefore, I do not welcome you; stay far away from me! / 27

7.13.m:
To him who spoke in this manner, O Vyāsa, Kaśyapa, enraged,
then spoke to that ruler of men, censuring the best of the Bhṛgus: / 32
“You are fallen, of bad conduct, broken in character, an extreme evildoer!
How can I perform the sacrifice for you, a perpetrator of the slaughter of embryos?” / 33
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, at those words, he said to the best of seers:
“Do not remain in my territory today, O best of sages! / 34
I am the master of the world, O brahmin; go where I am not.”
Then he, leaving his country, went away at that time; / 35
and he found no country where that powerful one was not master.
Finding none, he then took refuge in a forest,
and having become invisible, he wandered for many years. / 36
Then he saw a male pigeon perched on a tree,
bound by desire, captivated by a female pigeon. / 37
The male pigeon said:
“From the moment, O woman of shapely hips, you were seen by me, O fair one,
from that moment I wither away and find no pleasure, O lovely one!” / 38

7.13.m:
The female dove said:
“Never speak thus, wicked one! For it is contrary to dharma.”
The male dove said:
“If you will not give yourself to me here, O slender-waisted one, I will take you by force.
Yield to me; I bow down at your feet!”
The female dove said:
“Have you no fear, cruel one, of the mighty son of Jamadagni,
that today you violate here a faithful wife whose husband is away?”
Sanatkumāra said:
When addressed thus by her, that male dove, O son of Śakti,
said: “Who is this Rāma? Truly no one is my equal!”
As he was speaking thus there, an arrow inscribed with the name of Rāma
swiftly severed his head; and Kaśyapa witnessed that.

7.13.m:
Seeing what had thus occurred, frightened by that mighty one,
the high-minded [Kaśyapa] performed the sacrifice for the royal son of Jamadagni.
Kaśyapa said:
“I shall officiate at your sacrifice this very day, O king, best of the Bhṛgus,
if you will give me the auspicious sacrificial fee I desire.”
Rāma said:
“Whatever you say, of that there is no doubt: I shall give it, O you of great austerity.
Officiate at my sacrifice according to rule; today I remain under your control.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, took place his horse sacrifice of immense sacrificial fees,
in which the gods attained satisfaction.

Then, at the time of the sacrificial fee, the glorious son of Jamadagni
said to Kaśyapa: “Speak, what sacrificial fee may I give you?”
He replied: “Give to me as the sacrificial fee the entire earth, along with its mountains and forests,

7.13.m:
Kaśyapa said:
“Depart from this country and go to another country, sir!
You must not reside in my country today, O descendant of Bhṛgu.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Saying, “So be it,” and circumambulating him clockwise,
he went to the ocean, the source of rivers and abode of Varuṇa.
Having gone to that dreadful ocean, the descendant of Bhṛgu said:
“Grant me a region to dwell in, O great ocean!”
The ocean said:
“Proceed according to rule, since you now stand under my control.
Standing near the shore, draw your mighty bow,
and release an arrow, O Rāma, desiring an excellent land.
As far as that arrow, impelled by your strength, is cast
and reaches, just so far shall I grant your dwelling.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that tiger among the Bhṛgus, showing respect and unwearied,

7.13.m:
Then Śambhu was praised by the ocean to avert that,
for the welfare of the gods and to prevent the drying up of the ocean.
He arrested that matchless arrow released by the son of Jamadagni;
checked, having traversed only twelve yojanas, it fell down.
And as if laughing, the ocean ceded that much land,
and the son of Jamadagni of great splendor dwelt there accordingly.
The son of Bhṛgu, equal to the king of the gods, his soul rejoiced, made that region,
which was frequented by herds of deer and flocks of birds,
and resounded with the terrible roars of lions, mighty elephants, śarabhas, and bears, as prosperous as the city of the gods.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter in the Rāmamāhātmya of the Skandapurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
When the earth was thus given by the son of Jamadagni to the great-souled one,
she then sank downwards as if from the collapse of a mountain peak.
The sage angrily said to her: “Stay, stay, O bearer of wealth!
Why, having abandoned me, are you sinking downwards, O auspicious one?”
The earth said:
“Without Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, my dear husband of boundless splendor,
I cannot stay, O sage, my heart being captivated by his virtues.
If you do not grant me today to Rāma, O bull among sages,
I shall go down, O lord; I will not remain otherwise.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Hearing those words of hers, Kaśyapa, best of ascetics,
spoke angrily to the earth, as if burning [her] with his splendor:

The earth said: / O lord, through austerity, through yoga, and through strength, / no one at all is equal to you in heaven or on earth, O sovereign lord! (9)
I bow my head to win your favor; I have seen your supreme power. / Forgive whatever wrong I have done, O great sage! (10)
Indeed, by your command alone may I be the earth among the worlds. / Best of brahmins, you ought to show favor to me, who am wretched! (11)
Sanatkumāra said: / Seeing her thus positioned, the blessed one, the best of seers, / then smilingly spoke to the goddess, the earth who was bowed down: (12)
It was indeed because of your offense that this was done by me in such a manner. / Now perform the role of the earth granted by me! (13)
Attaining the status of my daughter, born of Kaśyapa's lineage, / you will be known in the world as Kāśyapī, O bearer of wealth! (14)
Sanatkumāra said: / Thus, Vyāsa, that earth, having gone down, stood firm again; / having regained the state of the earth, she became free from distress. (15)

7.13.m: Sanatkumāra said: / Hereafter I shall declare the mighty battle of the standard / of the gods and the asuras, which destroyed [their] vital breaths. (1) / There was a glorious, immensely powerful son of Danu named Vipracitti; / self-disciplined, he performed austerity at [the place called] Bhastrāpada, so it is heard. (2) / Having propitiated the lord of the gods, the blessed three-eyed one, / he chose the boon of immortality, and the guardian of the gods granted it to him. (3) / [He gave him] a divine, celestial standard, made of illusion, going everywhere, auspicious and golden. / And the blessed one, delighted in mind, said to the lord of the Dānavas: (4) / 'O son of Danu, this supreme all-formed standard belongs to you; / relying on it, you shall be invincible in battles, (5) / and immortal, O mighty-armed one, provided you do not utter a sound; / otherwise, your victory in battle will depend on your fortunes.' (6) / Addressed thus by the god, with that great standard in battle, / together with the Danavas, O best of brahmins, he challenged all the gods. (7)

7.13.m:
Focusing his aim upon the banner, the great-souled lord of the gods / struck down all those Dānavas, fourteen thousand in number.
Deafened by that roar, those mighty warriors who rivaled the king of the gods, / who bore emblems equal to Indra's, were struck down at the banner by the thunderbolt with the might of the king of gods.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, on the battle at the banner, in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.13.m:
Vyāsa said:
Bhastrāpada was mentioned by you, O imperishable son of Brahmā. / How did that place come to be? I wish to know this.
Sanatkumāra said:
Born in the Ikṣvāku lineage was a lord of subjects named Bāhu. / His entire kingdom was seized by force by the Haihayas and Tālajaṅghas, / O best of brahmins, and he went to the forest with his wife.
Having gone to Ṛcīka's hermitage and protected by Ṛcīka, / he dwelt in the middle of the forest together with his pregnant wife.
At the time of that wife's delivery, O son of Śakti, / poison was administered to her by her co-wife out of passion and delusion.
Afflicted with intense agony, burning and racked with pain, / she cried out, "Cold water!" and fell fainting to the ground.
Seeing her fallen thus, the king, tormented with grief, / although old, took a water jar and went to the river for water.
Having filled that jar and taken it upon his shoulder, sorrow-stricken, / he collapsed due to old age and exhaustion, and died.

7.13.m:
Afflicted by the burning of the poison and by the death of her husband, / she wailed like an osprey, O Vyāsa.
All the seers, headed by Vasiṣṭha, assembled for Bāhu; / having properly arranged the pyre, they approved the funeral rites.
As she, Śaivyā, entered that fire, being pregnant, / she was stopped by the seers and by the high-souled Aurva, O Vyāsa.
On that day at dusk, O Vyāsa, dispelling her grief, / that fetus emerged together with the poison (gara), radiant as fire.
The seer then gave him the name Sagara ('with poison'); / and, filled with compassion, performed all his life-cycle rites.
He also imparted to him the science of archery, the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, / a vast array of divine weapons, and an unhindered, imperishable chariot.

7.13.m:
With that foremost of chariots he slew the enemies in battle, / and, aiming the weapon of Aurva, destroyed their power.
Having slain them thus, O Vyāsa, and having regained the kingdom, / and having married the sister of Vainateya (Garuḍa) and the fair-waisted Śaivyā,
the mighty-armed king of great splendor, being childless, / worshipped Tryambaka, the best of the gods, for the sake of sons.
The blessed Lord granted him a son who would perpetuate the lineage, / and also sixty thousand high-souled sons.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having obtained the boon, the high-minded king spoke to his two wives, / the sister of Vainateya and Śaivyā.

7.13.m:
Sagara said:
The god has granted me one auspicious son who will perpetuate the lineage, / and sixty thousand high-souled sons.
Between the two, which auspicious, beneficial boon does each queen choose? / Speak, I will make no division for you, wise ones.
The sister of Vainateya said:
May sixty thousand sons be mine, O lord of men. / Śaivyā said: Let there be for me one son who will perpetuate the lineage.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Śaivyā gave birth to a son named Asamañja; / and the sister of Vainateya gave birth to a great gourd.
From that gourd then emerged those ten thousand, / multiplied by six, O Vyāsa, of mighty strength.

7.13.m:
Then the son Asamañja was abandoned by Sagara, / knowing him to be unrighteous and fixed in improper conduct.
His son Aṃśumat, however, was exceedingly righteous even as a child; / Sagara, the best of kings, then bestowed his affection upon him.
When Asamañja had been cast out, consecrated for a horse sacrifice, / he appointed those sixty thousand [sons] to guard the horse.
As those high-souled princes were attentively following the horse, / Śakra, having become invisible, stole that excellent horse away.
Having searched through all the worlds and not seeing the excellent horse, / they went to their consecrated father and reported the [loss of the] horse.

7.13.m: […] Then the king, enraged as if burning those sons, / with eyes red with anger, said: "Perish swiftly this very day! / Do not return without searching out the horse, you cruel ones! / What use are such sons as you to me? Go all of you to the realm of Yama!" / Sanatkumāra said: / Thus addressed, O best of brahmins, they then searched the entire three worlds, / and caused this whole earth to be dug up. / Having then seen the elephants of the directions and seers of strict vows, / holding the earth, seeing and bowing down to them all, / they perceived the sage Kapila sleeping in a pool of water, / and near him they saw the horse; then, enraged, they thought: / Driven by the destined end, ripe in time, wishing to die, / through their father's curse, they then spoke to Kapila, the best of sages: / "This wicked-minded one is the thief who stole our excellent horse and is asleep. / Let us all lead him today to our father's presence." / Sanatkumāra said: / Then, all bound by the noose of time, very mighty, / and under the control of destiny, they struck him with their feet. / Afflicted by them, he, enraged, then suddenly released / the breath held back for ten thousand years, like the king of serpents. / That breath, of the nature of fire, having issued from his mouth, / burned all the sons of Sagara, who were bereft of righteousness and virtue.

7.13.m: […] When they were all burned, the seers, headed by Nārada, / reported that exceedingly difficult event to Sagara as it happened. / Then that king, afflicted with grief, steadying himself by his own will, / the magnanimous one, commanded his beloved grandson Aṃśumat. / Sagara said: / "Ascending this chariot, go to that excellent horse; / bring it here, O mighty-armed one, so that our time [for the sacrifice] does not pass. / You must act according to the word of that best of seers, / so that he does not direct his anger at us; in you our lineage is established." / Sanatkumāra said: / Thus addressed, that king mounted his chariot, majestic, revered by gods and siddhas, / and went with speed, possessing the prowess of the king of gods, to where the yogin who brought an end to Sagara's sons shone. / Thus ends the one hundred twenty-sixth chapter, named 'The Origin of Sagara', in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.13.m:
They were not deliberately burned by me, O king, nor in wrath; / they were killed just as birds [are knocked down] by a fruit ripened by time. / This horse was placed beside me by someone who knew what he was doing, / taken for their destruction; do not be angry, let the horse be taken."
Sanatkumāra said: / With his permission, O Vyāsa, that king Aṃśumat, / the high-minded one, set about offering water for them. / The son of Vinatā said to him: "Water for my nephews / must not be offered [in this manner], O mighty-armed one; this will not reach them."
Aṃśumat said: / "How indeed may my fathers attain heavenly realms? / I wish this to be told by you, O son of Kaśyapa."
The son of Vinatā said: / "In the world of the gods there is a sacred river named Gaṅgā, remover of inauspiciousness. / If the bones of your kin here are in every way
touched by its waters, O king, then they may attain liberation / from inauspiciousness, O tiger among kings; otherwise, what use is [ordinary] water to them?"

Then the king’s anger toward the ocean was pacified. / And Viṣṇu, pleased with him at that time, granted him his desired boons:
A full hundred horse sacrifices, an imperishable abode in heaven, / eternal perpetuity of his lineage, and supreme, imperishable renown;
and also [divine] companionship, and supreme steadfastness in righteousness. / Having obtained these boons and enjoyed a kingdom free of rivals,
he went to the forest, and having performed austerity, went from there to heaven. / Then Aṃśumat shone forth as king, righteous and true to his promise.
Having consecrated his son in the kingdom, with the desire for the descent of the Gaṅgā, / he performed austerity and went to heaven, possessing great strength and prowess.
Then his son Dilīpa, great-souled, like the king of the gods, / having ruled the kingdom, O Vyāsa, went to the forest, endowed with great strength.

and constant victory in battle, as well as imperishable fame in the world; / and also the unequaled descent of the river Gaṅgā,
so that it may become known as “Bhāgīrathī” throughout the world: / “This I desire, O Lord of gods, if you deem it proper, O Almighty!”
Sanatkumāra said:
Addressed thus, the venerable Creator himself granted him all this / without remainder, and said this to the king:
“You, O tiger among kings, will lead the Gaṅgā from heaven to the surface of the earth. / Yet no one is capable of holding her as she falls from heaven,
except the divine Guru of the world, Tryambaka, who holds the trident in his hand.
Therefore, worship the God of gods with steadfast vows; / the all-pervading Lord will manifest and surely hold her by granting your boon.”
Sanatkumāra said: / Addressed thus, the king of kings lived on air, unblinking, / and held his breath there on the auspicious peak of the Himālaya.

Hearing his words, the Lord whose banner bears the bull / spoke to the tiger among kings with a thoroughly delighted mind:

Sanatkumāra said: / Noticing that perturbation, the gods spoke to Śatakratu: / "This upheaval has not arisen without cause; let it be understood quickly, O lord!" / And that deity fell into delusion, together with the seers. / At that moment Brahmā arrived and enlightened them.
Brahmā said: / "Do not stand despondent, all you denizens of heaven! / Understand what I say; let this time not slip past you.
This god, the great archer, he of the matted hair, who rides the clouds, / of terrifying prowess, has resolved to destroy Gaṅgā. / Since the god has thus devised in his mind [a scheme] destructive to the world, / act without delay so that disaster may not happen!

7.13.m:
Sanatkumāra said: / Then the gods, accompanied by Brahmā, the lotus-born, / went to the peak of the Himālaya, adorned with all kinds of jewels, / named Hiraṇmaya, where flows the river Hairaṇvatī; / and through their devotion and austerity, the gods beheld the lord of the gods.
Sanatkumāra said: / Seeing him appearing enraged, glowing like the fire at the end of the world-age, / hard to look upon, then, O Vyāsa, they took refuge with the Devī. / The gods said: / "You are the mother of the worlds together with their deities, O radiant one! / Therefore you are our protectress, O Rudrāṇī; grant us the station that gives fearlessness!
"We have come for refuge, O Mother; we are your children, O auspicious one! / Protect us, O queen of the god of gods; this is what we desire."
Sanatkumāra said: / Hearing their words, the Devī granted fearlessness / and an unsurpassed boon to the gods who were terrified and sought refuge.
Then, having bowed with her head to the blessed Pināka-wielder, the lord of the god of gods, / the daughter of the mountain, affectionate to the terrified, spoke:

7.13.m:
Sanatkumāra said: / The god then raised her with his hand that had the lustre of a lotus petal, / as she was bowed down in fear, her hair falling at his feet.
And he said to the virtuous lady: "You are frightened, O daughter of the Himālaya! / Why, and what is your fear, O fair-browed one? Speak, O lovely-faced one!"
[Variant readings: 51 ...māgatām (ka.); 52 rgajata (ka.); 53 ...bjatalatviṣā (ka.).] / 704 / Sanatkumāra said: / Then, O Vyāsa, the daughter of the Himālaya spoke to him as one terrified: / "I am exceedingly frightened, O God, seeing your intensely blazing form,
"resembling the fire of dissolution, difficult to look upon even for the gods. / The worlds are despondent, O lord of gods, and so are the gods together with the seers.
"Full of fear, all these lords of the gods pay homage to you. / I am afraid of you, O Mahādeva, and these gods are even more afraid than I.
"And they have sought refuge in me; grant them freedom from fear! / You are the creator of all the worlds and of the gods together with the seers. / Do not destroy them after creating them! Bowing with my head, I beseech you."

7.13.m:
Sanatkumāra said: / Hearing her words and seeing the gods, the destroyer of the sacrifice / said: "You have no fear from me, O best of the thirty [gods]!
"However, by her womanly nature, this river, daughter of the Himālaya, / harboring an evil intent toward me, will fall upon me.
"I will restrain that river falling from the sky. / You too, O sinless ones, go to your respective abodes with confidence!" / Sanatkumāra said: / Then, hearing his words, those foremost of immortals bowed down / and, folding their hands in reverence, said with a modest voice:
The gods said: / "This best of rivers was created by you for the welfare of the world. / Rivers are fickle, and such is the nature of women.
"Because of that nature and because of having recourse to us, / she has assumed great arrogance and boasts, fearing nothing from anywhere.

7.13.m:
For when anyone in the world is solicited for the sake of some purpose, / he becomes proud, even if he is insignificant, O Lord; what then of this best of rivers?
This river, O Mahādeva, desired by you to be borne, / proud because you are the supreme god among all, therefore boasts.
When she, the best of rivers, is borne by you, the Lord of gods, / she will become auspicious in this world, destroying all sins.
Any [other] god, O Lord of deities, might be capable / of bearing this falling river, but no higher welfare would come from it.
Therefore you are entreated by the gods and by this king, O slayer of Kāla: / becoming benevolent, O best of gods, bear this river!
Sanatkumāra said:
When the Lord, the God, was thus addressed by the gods along with Brahmā / and Nārāyaṇa, the guardians of the world, with words that were true, abundant, and irreproachable,
and considering again and again the bestowing of the boon upon the king, / the Lord of gods spoke this to the gods with a deep voice:

The gods said:
“O Blessed One, we desire a place of the God of great prosperity: / the sacred field Samantapañcaka has been forever abandoned by you.
Since she was called ‘Bhastrā’ by us, the imperishable daughter of Himavat, / and they desire a place of safety, therefore it is known as Bhastrāpada.
Whoever, restrained by vows, should come here and worship the Bull-bannered One, / having obtained the fruit of a horse sacrifice, would reach the world of Rudra.
And whoever offers a caru oblation with a fast of a day and night, / he shall become equal to Nandīśvara, O best of gods.
And whatever man here abandons his vital breaths, O Lord of gods, observed by vows, / or even without vows, O God, by a death by chance,
he too, becoming equal to the Gaṇas, will remain until the dissolution of all beings, / endowed with a divine body, having attained attendance upon you.
And whoever, always pure, says, ‘Homage to Bhastreśvara,’ / whether rising up or sleeping, he rejoices in the world of Śakra.

and another tīrtha of Yama, then another tīrtha of Vāyu, / and yet another tīrtha of Viṣṇu, renowned and worshipped by the gods.

7.13.m:
The God of Gods said: / “Bhagīratha, where is that Gaṅgā who delivers your ancestors? / Summon her, O mighty-armed one! I will receive her, no doubt.” / Sanatkumāra said: / Then that tiger among kings, remembering that word of Brahmā, / remembered the river, O Vyāsa, bowing down with folded hands and bent head. / Called in thought by him, the river whose abode was the celestial world, / the goddess who brings auspiciousness, arrived in an instant at Bhuvarloka. / Having reached that world, the river, swift as the wind and mind, / exceedingly rapid, bringing hundreds of blessings, adorned everything.
Then, having descended obliquely, standing in space, the great river / became known as Ākāśagaṅgā, and indeed by the name Oghavatī.
That great river, Ākāśagaṅgā, rushing with immense speed, / thought, ‘May it be auspicious for me!’ and descending along midway of its course, / was therefore called Śivagaṅgā by name, for it is most auspicious.

7.13.m: Making an immense sound like the crash of a thunderbolt, / because she was seen alongside the gods, she is therefore called Devagaṅgā. / Having seen her, all the sages and all the realms of the gods / immediately chanted peace prayers, their bodily hairs bristling with joy. / As they were chanting, O Vyāsa, that river that brings happiness to the worlds, / praising as if terrified, divided into three and fell to the earth. / As she fell with immense speed in three torrents, / Mahādeva caught her with his mass of matted hair in the very presence of the gods. / Having reached that mass of matted locks, the three-streamed river became subdued; / restrained by his yogic power, she did not reach its end. / Because she fell terrified and offering praise, / she is therefore called Bhītagaṅgā and Stotragaṅgā. / And because that best of rivers fell in three torrents, / she is called Trisrotā by those who expound the Veda. / Sanatkumāra said: / Having fallen onto him and held by the god through his mystic power, / searching for an opening in the matted locks, she remained there for many years. / As she dwelt for a full thousand years in the abode of his matted hair, / all the gods saw her as if lodged inside the hollow of a tree. / Then those gods quickly bowed down to the one who bears a bull on his banner / and said despondently, O Vyāsa: ‘Do not destroy the river!’”

7.13.m:
As he shook out the mass of matted hair, drops indeed fell there. / Resembling pearls, pure as the rays of the full moon, (45) / they formed the divine Bindusaras, radiant like an ocean. / From it seven great streams flowed forth: (46)
Nalinī, Hlādinī, and Plāvanī going eastward, / and Sītā, Cakṣus, and Sindhu, those three going westward. (47)
King Bhagīratha followed the middle stream, where / that Gaṅgā is called Bhāgīrathī by those who know the Veda. (48)
Splitting [the ground], the best of rivers went towards the Himavat; / she was obstructed at the foot of the Himavat on a jewel-peaked mountain of stone. (49)
Then, seeing her obstructed, King Bhagīratha, with a dejected face, / remembered Brahmā in his mind, O Vyāsa. (50)
Then the lord Brahmā said to the great elephant Supratīka: / “Split this mountain of stone with your two adamantine tusks!” (51)

7.13.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim in full the Hālāhala [war], / the terrifying battle between the sons of Diti and the gods. (1)
A host known as Hālāhala, heroic in prowess, / terrible, a thorn to Brahmā, shone among the asuras, O Vyāsa. (2)
When the sons of Danu were gone, that host, swooning with rage, / placing their forces at the vanguard, challenged all the gods to battle. (3)
A most terrible battle took place between them, / and victory always fell to the asuras. (4)
Then all the gods, their pride gone and prowess shattered, / their kingdom taken away, approached Brahmā, the cause of the worlds. (5)
Having gathered together, they said to him: “Now our kingdom is taken away! / How, O god, might we regain the kingdom through your splendor?” (6)
Having heard those words of theirs, the god born from the waters / said to the gods: “Propitiate the Lord of the gods without delay! (7)
That god of great valor, the Three-eyed One, will give you strength / by which you will conquer all of them in battle through prowess.” (8)

7.13.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Being addressed thus, the gods, having propitiated Śaṅkara, the Lord of gods, with austerity, / with folded hands said: “Give us strength, O destroyer of the sacrifice!” (9)
Gratified by the austerity of those chanting thus, Hara / then gave an unassailable mantra, the best of all mantras. (10)
Having obtained that, O brahmin seer, the celestials, their protection secured, / though wise, all behaved like fools among the asuras. (11)
Then the wicked asuras, seeing all the celestials appearing foolish, / thought: “They are indeed fools, just as they seem! (12)
Deprived of their kingdom, these gods, with minds bewildered, / wander about like madmen. Look at them, O enemies of the gods!” (13)
Others reviled them, and struck them terribly; / some bound them as they pleased, and others set them free. (14)

7.13.m:
Thus, as those of auspicious deeds acted in this way, O Vyāsa, / their virtue became very great, while that of the asuras perished. (15)
Because of that misconduct of the evil-minded asuras, / and the loss of virtue, their strength was depleted—this the hosts of gods realized. (16)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, addressed by Brahmā, all of them bearing divine weapons, / summoned the tiger-like asuras to battle and slaughtered them all, (17)
where Bala was slain in battle by the hundred-jointed thunderbolt
by the lord of gods having advanced with prowess—hence he is remembered as Balahan. (18)
Sanatkumāra said:
There was another most fearful war, the Andhakāraka [war], / which lasted for ten thousand years and ten hundred more. (19)

7.13.m: […] / 716 / "This woman with all lovely limbs is mine, not yours, O fair-waisted one! / Or rather, let her be the prize of battle: release her and strike me!" // 43 // / Having spoken various words like this, the Daiteyas, driven by death, / brought about mutual slaughter and went to the abode of Yama. // 44 // / And those Dānavas surviving the slaughter whose valor was shattered / were all slain in battle by the gods of fierce splendor. // 45 // / Whosoever of purified mind reads of this destruction of the lords of the Dānavas in an assembly, / that mortal man shall obtain in this very world young women resembling the apsarases. // 46 // / Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in the battle of darkness.

7.13.m: Vyāsa said: / How was that daitya Andhaka struck down by Hara, / under whose power the entire three worlds lay out of fear? // 1 // / Sanatkumāra said: / The lord of daityas named Andhaka was at first a thorn to the three worlds. / Having obtained boons from Brahmā, he was invulnerable to gods and mortals. // 2 // / When he was enraged in battle, neither Viṣṇu, nor Śakra, nor Yama / was able to stand facing him; how much less the other gods? // 3 // / Once, puffed up with pride in his strength, roaming about this earth, / he saw on a ridge of Mount Mandara the goddess, the daughter of Himavat. // 4 // / Beholding her, the lord of daityas, his mind ruined by desire, / thinking, "I alone am the master," conceived wickedness toward the goddess. // 5 // / And having thought so, he spoke to the Dānavas following him: / "Quickly bring this daughter of the mountain near to me!" // 6

Hearing those words of his whose mind was possessed by desire, / Prahlāda, the best of speakers, spoke these words: // 7
"O lord of the Dānavas, words that are beneficial and clear in the outcome / must certainly be spoken by me, especially out of love for a kinsman. // 8
She is the daughter of Himavat, the wife of the wise Śarva. / You must not ponder wickedness toward her, lest she burn us with her splendor! // 9
Toward the goddess, the mother of the universe, who is worthy of worship and of blinding splendor, / toward Umā, O tiger among the Dānavas, you must not offer insult here. // 10
Having bound a huge rock to your neck with a foolish mind, / do you wish to cross a dreadful river full of deep whirlpools? // 11

Having become a moth, out of delusion, do you wish to touch / the blazing flame of fire for your destruction, O sovereign of the Dānavas? // 12 // / Do not lead everyone, roots and all, to destruction, O lord of the Dānavas! / Turn your mind away from the goddess; this is not fitting for the wise. // 13
You are wise, noble, and born of the lineage of the highborn; / a performer of sacrifices and constantly devoted to dharma—this is not fitting for you, O lord! // 14
You have many women, all of enduring youth, / naturally of beautiful limbs; let your mind be turned back from the goddess! // 15
To him who, pleased with our austerity, grants desired boons— / toward that God of gods' consort, you wish to commit sin! // 16
He by whom Dakṣa, the sacrifice, death, and desire were brought to destruction— / from that God of gods, you wish to seize half his body! // 17 // / The God who is worshipped in liṅgas by gods, asuras, and great serpents— / how can you disrespect his goddess, the sustainer of the world? // 18

7.13.m: Thousands of Pramathas, yogins of terrifying deeds, / march before him, just like your Dānavas before you. // 20 // / He who could rob the sun of its brilliance, the moon of its loveliness, the earth of its patience, / or Vāsuki of his fang—he might rob him of Pārvatī! // 21 // / The whole head of him shall shatter into a hundred fragments, / whatever fool would insult that noble wife of Śarva. // 22 // / What you were told back then by the grandfather, born from the lotus, / at the end of the granting of the boon—you ought to remember those words: // 23 // / 'This fortune, O son of Diti, which was granted by me, so very hard to attain— / through your own bad conduct alone, O Dānava, it will pass elsewhere.' // 24 // / Those who, gripped by folly, do not listen to the words of kinsmen / that are wholesome though bitter, those men go to their doom. // 25 // / We shall approach the god Śaṃkara for your sake; / having met [in battle], we shall all meet together in the abode of Yama." // 26 // / Addressed thus with wholesome words by that kinsman, / he, impelled by time, said laughing, "It is not so! // 27 // / In this unavoidable matter, whether proper or improper, which is dear to me, / if there should be destruction for me in battle, even destruction is my victory. // 28

Then, instructed by the goddess, with various weapons in their hands, / they faced the Dānavas, led by Somanandin. // 32 // / Having fought a great battle with the Dānava followers, / they were scattered by the lord of the Dānavas like clouds by the wind. // 33 // / In the meantime, the goddess, seeing that Andhaka advancing fiercely, / ran forward herself, taking up a bow with arrows. // 34
She struck Andhaka between his breasts with twenty-five / sharp-pointed arrows; he fainted and fell. // 35 // / Then, recovering his senses in a moment, out of pride the Dānava / rose up swiftly with speed, his terrible bow raised high. // 36
Then rising again, that great asura against the goddess / loosed showers of arrows, like a rain cloud pouring rain. // 37 // / Then, as she raised her trident, possessing the brilliance of blazing fire, / and began to slay Andhaka, the God gently restrained her: // 38
"This lord of the Dānavas is to be chastised by me alone; do not exert yourself! / I myself will pierce his heart with the trident in battle." // 39

7.13.m:
[…]
[Nandin said:]
“The eternal beings, chosen and distinguished, were created by you yourself at creation,
whose manifold nature as subjects is indeed difficult to describe.
Having bull-banners, bull-chariots, and crescent moons as ornaments,
these Rudras, dear to you, O Rudra, have arrived together.
One hundred times a hundred thousand times ten million is the number of these great souls,
and just as many thousands and hundreds, O all-pervading lord.

And sixty thousand of these blue-throated gods,
these great-souled blue-throated ones, to whom there is no equal.
These heroes, fierce in power, of fierce and lofty prowess,
will gladden your heart as they fight.
Matching these very Rudras in power,
are the doorkeepers of that very measure, valorous, having conquered wrath.
Thus, having monkey and lion faces, possessing the strength of monkeys and lions in battle,
they will fight with the Dānavas like elephants against elephants.

7.13.m:
And the Rudras, the sons of the Rudras, and the attendants of the Rudras—
O lord of Rudras, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished by them.
To each of these Rudras, O best of those who have sons,
there are five sons each, of great valor, wearing sidelocks.
Those who were born suddenly from your arms, sprung from your anger,
putting Vīrabhadra at their head, have arrived here.
Sixty crores and sixteen thousand
of these troop leaders, dear to you, O lord of troops, have come here.
Thus, O god, for the sake of your pleasure, Dakṣa’s prosperous sacrifice
was destroyed by them; O destroyer of the cities, O god, behold them arrived once more!

resembling mountains of fire, thirty crores of these troop leaders
have arrived to please you, O sinless Maheśvara.
These wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and ointments,
born from the blood of your lip, are troop leaders named the Raktas.
Followers of Aṅgāraka, of great power and prowess,
sixty thousand crores of them have arrived.
Nor should this alone be considered their strength by you, O sinless one;
for they possess the eightfold sovereignty born from your grace, O god.
Displaying it, O Maheśāna, they could reduce to ashes many worlds,
active with gods, Asuras, and mortals,
and the gods and Dānavas in battle down to the end of the yuga.
These who resemble jasmine flowers, adorned with golden blue-lotuses,
armored, O lord of troops, all eager for battle,
pious toward brahmins, these heroes adorned with the crescent moon,
the Rudras, O lord of Rudras, have arrived; behold them longing for battle!

shining in form like many risen moons,
wearing sidelocks, shaved-headed, standing on roosters,
these are the youths named Śākhas of renowned valor.
These who ride goats and rams, having the luster of kiṃśuka and aśoka flowers,
heroic and generous, with faces like young lotuses,
having equipment matching that of your son Naigameṣa,
these, O god, are the youths known as Naigameṣas.
These who resemble dark rain-clouds, roaring like dark rain-clouds,
are your Pramathas born from your hair, O god, who have arrived.
And these are many red troops, crushers of hostile forces,
possessing chariot-guards, armored, charioteers, diverse warriors,
all with various weapons, all skilled in war,
accomplished, intoxicated with battle, and all clad in armor;
having the hue of white and dark clouds and of mountains,
violent like oceans with crocodiles, fish, and sea-monsters.

7.13.m: […] / These heroic attendants of Skanda, the supreme soul, / given by the gods as playmates, have approached you from all sides. / The fierce, rejoiced, and mighty army of Pramathas, O Īśvara, / is capable of breaking the ranks of the Dānavas—this is my thought. / Abandoning other matters, showing supreme respect, / bring destruction without delay to the misfortune of the gods' enemies. / Shining like elephants, mountains, trees, and arched gateways, equal in splendour to the youthful sun, / these leaders of your gaṇas, O Īśvara, are prepared to conquer the enemy force. / O Lord of the moving and unmoving, then Andhaka standing in battle will meet his match. / Surrounded by hosts of hundreds of Gaṇapatis, send forth, O Lord, the bowed masters of the gaṇas. / Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, on the preparation for the battle with Andhaka, in the Skandapurāṇa.

[…] / he spoke with a voice rumbling like a cloud, resounding like a hundred kettledrums: / "You, O best of beings, are fit to fight with the Dānavas for me. / You alone, leaders of the gaṇas, are sufficient to oppress them. / Therefore, O beings of great vigor, along with your hosts and your followers, / march forth for their destruction; I am pleased [with you], O beings of great might!"
Thus addressed by the God, bowing with their heads to Hara, / the great-souled ones departed, and the God also set forth. / Then a roar arose like an ocean being cleft open, / as the army of the asura Andhaka approached Mandara. / Hearing the roar of the Dānavas, which intensely strained the ears, / the Pramathas roared dreadfully like clouds at the end of an age. / Those two oceanic armies, stirred up by each other's might, / became like two great oceans stirred and cleft open at the end of dissolution.

The Dānavas, though checked by the Pramathas who seemed victorious, / broke through the Pramatha army and then quickly climbed up.
The Pramathas, having resolved that battle must be fought without attachment, / slashed, pierced, and split the enemies of the gods. / "Seize! Release! Stand! What will you do standing there?"— / thus words arose between the armies of Pramathas and asuras. / With excellent trees, roots and all, and with mountains complete with trees, / the merciless Pramathas and asuras crushed one another.

7.13.m: Then, by the sons of Dākṣāyaṇī, the destroyers of Dakṣa's sacrifice, / unwavering in their devotion, could not be turned back. / Sanatkumāra said: / Perceiving that the enemies, defeated, were unable / to climb the summit of the mountain, the God restrained the Pramathas completely. / The God of gods said: / "Let the sons of Danu climb Mandara with its lovely caves. / For my sport, O lords of the gaṇas, fight together with them!" / They saw [the mountain] where a terrible roar was uttered by the king of beasts standing in many lovely bowers, / whose ground was strewn with the flowers of trees broken by the charges of herds of roaming elephants, / where the darkness of lovely rock caverns was dispelled by the lamps of the crest jewels of serpent kings, / and whose clefts were seen among networks of great rocks split by the speed of cool, clear torrent water.

7.13.m:
Then, being let through by the Pramathas, the sons of Diti climbed up, / thinking that the Pramathas, terrified, had quickly retreated. / Then on the top of Mandara, thick with various trees, / the Daityas stood, massed together, possessing the radiance of the sun.
Mount Mandara, with its terrible rocks, stones, and trees, its grown tigers, hyenas, and elephants, / was violently overwhelmed by the great Asuras with their proud steeds and elephants, like a cloud by the winds.
In some places they hurled stones resembling white clouds; tearing up trees, they roared like clouds; / when opposed, they crushed the Pramathas, as lions [crush] the leaders of herds of deer in the forests.

7.13.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Reaching the slopes of Mandara, Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas,
with folded hands addressed Śukra, who possessed splendour like Indra and the sun: // 1
Andhaka said:
"O Lord, we have reached Mount Mandara with its lovely caves,
whose rocky surfaces are barred by frightful Pramathas. // 2
Moving through the air, masters of illusion, and yogins of great might,
these leaders of the gaṇas cannot be overcome by the Dānavas by brute force alone. // 3
Usually, even powerful good men proceed in their undertakings
first by means of strategy, and only later otherwise. // 4
Therefore, resorting to a strategy, particularly focused,
let us harass the Pramathas, or whatever pleases you. // 5

who stand amidst the ranks of the Pramathas and gaze repeatedly at me?" // 7

7.13.m:
He who, having mounted a calling peacock with variegated plumage,
shines with the radiance of the morning sun, holding a spear in his hand, of great might, // 13
beneficent to brahmins, devoted to the sacred knowledge, a celibate observing his vows—
this is Skanda, the leader of the gods, O Dānavas, in battle. // 14
He who stands on a red-crested rooster, radiant like a red-crested mountain stone,
brandishing a spear, shines like a raincloud [brandishing] lightning, // 15
this one wearing youthful sidelocks, with a face resembling the full moon,
is named Viśākha, a youth observant of youthful celibacy. // 16
Youthful, possessed of fresh intelligence, like a tree endowed with branches,
this son of Svāhā, endowed with great splendour, is named Śākha. // 17
And the one who stands flanking his right side,
repeatedly pointing his forefinger at me and at you, // 18
mounted on a ram, a mighty child standing firm—
he is known as Naigameṣa, O Andhaka, the son of Hara. // 19

Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to the Dānava lord and the Dānavas, the descendant of Bhṛgu
then began to marshal that army into the mountain array. // 23
Having placed Andhaka's chariot at the base, along with Andhaka, his horses, and his charioteer,
he made its foothills out of many thousands of foot soldiers. // 24
Along those thousands of feet of the mountain array, the descendant of Bhṛgu
had heaps of trees, rocks, and boulders made by the Dānavas. // 25
With a hundred million of those high-souled Dānavas
with copper-coloured eyes, the lord of planets fashioned its slopes. // 26
Upon the slopes variegated by mineral streams, the descendant of Bhṛgu
stationed Dānavas like grass and shrubs. // 27
And with three hundred million of those enemies of the lord of the thirty gods,
he whose radiance equalled the sun fashioned the peaks of the mountain array. // 28

those armed Dānavas, saying: "These are the precipices." // 29

Hasti and Duryodhana, and Pāka and the Dānava Dhundhu— / these and other mighty Daityas, thorns to the gods—
‘Protect the battle-array! Fight!’ so spoke the lord of the Asuras. / Like Himavān, the king of mountains, or the Vindhya with its wondrous caverns,
that mountain-array shone forth, its trees bristling with weapons, / like darkness gathered into one place, like a mass of clouds. / Seeing again and again the mountain-array, the Pramathas were astonished, / looking upon the mountain-array while stationed in their own mountain-array.
Those tigers among the Asuras roared like clouds at the destruction of the world, / and they said: ‘This [array] cannot be broken even by the gods together with Indra!

( 733 ) / In the center of the thunderbolt-array, standing in a magnificent chariot, / stood the Lord, Bhava, Śarva, Kapardin, Nīlalohita.
His great white banner shone like Indra’s banner, / like the Mandara mountain whose peak is embraced by the orb of the moon.
With a hundred edges, many joints, and a beautifully adorned bud, / the thunderbolt-array seemed eager to shatter the mountain-array.

Then among the forces of the lord of Gaṇas, lion-roars arose, / mingled with the sounds of paṇavas, mṛdaṅgas, and conches,
bringing terror to the sons of Diti, / like the roar of clouds over an agitated ocean.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled ‘The Formation of Battle-Arrays,’ in the Slaying of Andhaka in the Skandapurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: / Having seen those two arrays devised by the Pramathas and the Asuras, the gods / swiftly blocked the sky on all sides with crores of aerial chariots.
The entire vault of heaven, strewn with radiance, shone / like the lovely peak-forest of Meru being consumed by fire.
Filled with the sound of celestial drums, crowded with hundreds of divine women, / that assembly of gods shone forth just like the solar disc.
Strewn with divine blossoms, perfumed with celestial scents, / and filled with onlookers by the hundreds, the heavenly expanse of the sky shone brightly.
